claims.text: There is a small but statistically significant correlation between social media use and depressive symptoms in children and adolescents.
The random-effects pooled correlation estimate between social media use and depressive symptoms across cross-sectional studies is r = 0.12.
The random-effects pooled correlation estimate between social media use and depressive symptoms across longitudinal studies is r = 0.12.
Trimming and filling outlying studies reduces the random-effects pooled correlation estimate between social media use and depressive symptoms to r = 0.09.

evidence.description: The overall random effects pooled estimate was 0.13 (0.05, 0.2), p = 0.001; Q = 131.47, df = 10, p = < 0.0001, I2 = 92.4%.
The pooled estimate for cross-sectional studies (n = 6) was r = 0.12, (95% CI 0.02, 0.22), Q = 81.01, I2 = 93.8%.
The pooled estimate for longitudinal studies (n = 5) was r = 0.12, (95% -0.01, 0.25), Q = 38.98, I2 = 89.7%.

Trim and fill analysis showed two outlying studies, trimming and filling of which resulted in a random effects estimate of r = 0.09 (95% CI 0.01, 0.16), p = 0.03; Q = 180.67, df = 12, p < 0.0001, I2 = 93.4%.

methodologies.name: Systematic Review and Random-Effects Meta-Analysis
methodologies.description: Systematic search of Medline, PsycInfo, and Embase databases yielding 11 eligible studies (N=12,646), followed by meta-analysis using Fisher's z transformation and DerSimonian-Laird random-effects estimator in R.
conditions: Correlations converted using compute.es package in R

methodologies.name: Euclidean Cluster Analysis
methodologies.description: Agglomerative Euclidean cluster analysis conducted on correlation results to categorize study outcome patterns.
datasets: Extracted correlation metrics from 11 included studies

limitations.text: The total number of eligible studies focused specifically on social media use and depressive symptoms was low (n = 11), limiting the collated evidence base.
Wide heterogeneity in design, sample size, measurement instruments, and results across included studies tempers any firm conclusions.
Only English-language studies were included due to lack of translation resources, introducing potential selection bias.
Over half of the reviewed studies were cross-sectional, and longitudinal designs were restricted to short durations (maximum 12 months).
Prior studies exhibit a high risk of bias due to reliance on self-report, unvalidated measurement tools, and lack of exclusion of existing depression cases.

future_work.text: Qualitative methods should be utilized to gain an in-depth understanding of the mental health impact of social media from young people's own perspectives.
Researchers must establish consensus on variables and measurement definitions to enable consistent replication.
Exploration of using profiling data from online social communication in healthcare risk assessment contexts for early identification of wellbeing concerns.
Investigation into how the relationship with social media evolves through developmental stages as user experience grows.
